claim: PERK signaling is a component of the mouse MAP kinase neuronal stress response controlled by DLK.
source: Here we show that PERK signaling is a component of the mouse MAP kinase neuronal stress response controlled by the Dual Leucine Zipper Kinase (DLK) and contributes to DLK-mediated neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: PERK signaling contributes to DLK-mediated neurodegeneration.
source: Here we show that PERK signaling is a component of the mouse MAP kinase neuronal stress response controlled by the Dual Leucine Zipper Kinase (DLK) and contributes to DLK-mediated neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: DLK-activating insults ranging from nerve injury to neurotrophin deprivation result in JNK signaling.
source: We find that DLK-activating insults ranging from nerve injury to neurotrophin deprivation result in both c-Jun N-terminal Kinase (JNK) signaling and the PERK- and ISR-dependent upregulation of the Activating Transcription Factor 4 (ATF4).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: DLK-activating insults ranging from nerve injury to neurotrophin deprivation result in PERK- and ISR-dependent upregulation of ATF4.
source: We find that DLK-activating insults ranging from nerve injury to neurotrophin deprivation result in both c-Jun N-terminal Kinase (JNK) signaling and the PERK- and ISR-dependent upregulation of the Activating Transcription Factor 4 (ATF4).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Disruption of PERK signaling delays neurodegeneration without reducing JNK signaling.
source: Disruption of PERK signaling delays neurodegeneration without reducing JNK signaling.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: DLK is sufficient for PERK activation.
source: Furthermore, DLK is both sufficient for PERK activation and necessary for engaging the ISR subsequent to JNK-mediated retrograde injury signaling.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: DLK is necessary for engaging the ISR subsequent to JNK-mediated retrograde injury signaling.
source: Furthermore, DLK is both sufficient for PERK activation and necessary for engaging the ISR subsequent to JNK-mediated retrograde injury signaling.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: PERK is thought to be engaged in models of neurodegenerative diseases as one of four eukaryotic initiation factor 2 alpha (eIF2α) kinases.
source: One such pathway is the Integrated Stress Response (ISR), which is thought to be engaged in models of neurodegenerative diseases by PERK, one of four eukaryotic initiation factor 2 alpha (eIF2α) kinases (Halliday and Mallucci, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Halliday and Mallucci, 2014.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α suppresses general translation but enhances the translation of select mRNAs, including Atf4, Ppp1r15a, and Ddit3.
source: The resulting phosphorylation of eIF2α suppresses general translation but enhances the translation of select mRNAs, including that of the Activating transcription factor-4 (Atf4), Protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 15A (Ppp1r15a, which encodes the protein Gadd34), and DNA damage-inducible transcript-3 (Ddit3, which encodes the protein CHOP) (Palam et al., 2011; Wek et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Palam et al., 2011 and Wek et al., 2006.

claim: Disrupting PERK signaling is neuroprotective in models of Alzheimer's disease, prion diseases, and other disorders involving protein aggregation.
source: Disrupting PERK signaling is neuroprotective in models of Alzheimer's disease (AD), prion diseases, and other disorders involving protein aggregation (Halliday et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2013; Matus et al., 2013; Moreno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Halliday et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2013; Matus et al., 2013; Moreno et al., 2013.

claim: PERK is stimulated by endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and initiates the ISR as one of the three branches of the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR).
source: Canonically, PERK is stimulated by endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and initiates the ISR as one of the three branches, along with IRE1α and ATF6α, of the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) (Wek et al., 2006), although the upstream regulators of PERK activation in the context of disease have not yet been determined.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wek et al., 2006.

claim: The upstream regulators of PERK activation in the context of disease have not yet been determined.
source: Canonically, PERK is stimulated by endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and initiates the ISR as one of the three branches, along with IRE1α and ATF6α, of the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) (Wek et al., 2006), although the upstream regulators of PERK activation in the context of disease have not yet been determined.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: Components and regulators of the UPR, including phosphorylated PERK, phosphorylated IRE1α, CHOP, and Luman, have been noted after nerve damage.
source: Components and regulators of the UPR, including phosphorylated PERK, phosphorylated IRE1α, CHOP, and the ATF6-related transcription factor Luman, have recently been noted after nerve damage, with Luman serving a pro-regenerative role (Hu et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2016; Ying et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2016; Ying et al., 2015.

claim: Luman serves a pro-regenerative role after nerve damage.
source: Components and regulators of the UPR, including phosphorylated PERK, phosphorylated IRE1α, CHOP, and the ATF6-related transcription factor Luman, have recently been noted after nerve damage, with Luman serving a pro-regenerative role (Hu et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2016; Ying et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2016; Ying et al., 2015.

claim: Following neurotrophin deprivation or axonal damage, DLK stabilization leads to the activation of JNK2 and JNK3.
source: Following neurotrophin deprivation or axonal damage, DLK stabilization leads to the activation of the stress-responsive c-Jun N-terminal kinases JNK2 and JNK3 (Sengupta Ghosh et al., 2011; Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013; Tedeschi and Bradke, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sengupta Ghosh et al., 2011; Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013; Tedeschi and Bradke, 2013.

claim: Phosphorylation of c-Jun downstream of JNK2 and JNK3 leads to the induction of multiple regeneration-associated genes.
source: Downstream of JNK2 and JNK3 kinase activity, phosphorylation of the AP-1 transcription factor c-Jun leads to the induction of multiple regeneration-associated genes, and this pathway is required for robust axon regrowth after peripheral nerve injury (Fernandes et al., 2013; Raivich et al., 2004; Shin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2013; Raivich et al., 2004; Shin et al., 2012.

claim: The DLK/JNK/c-Jun pathway is required for robust axon regrowth after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Downstream of JNK2 and JNK3 kinase activity, phosphorylation of the AP-1 transcription factor c-Jun leads to the induction of multiple regeneration-associated genes, and this pathway is required for robust axon regrowth after peripheral nerve injury (Fernandes et al., 2013; Raivich et al., 2004; Shin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2013; Raivich et al., 2004; Shin et al., 2012.

claim: c-Jun is necessary for the upregulation of Gadd45a mRNA that is important for neuronal survival after peripheral nerve damage.
source: For instance, it is necessary for the upregulation of the UPR-associated mRNA Gadd45a that is important for neuronal survival after peripheral nerve damage (Fernandes et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2011.

claim: c-Jun contributes to the expression of pro-apoptotic genes including Ddit3 and Atf3 that contribute to the death of axotomized retinal ganglion cells following optic nerve crush.
source: c-Jun also contributes to the expression of a number of pro-apoptotic genes, including the UPR-associated mRNAs Ddit3 and Atf3 that contribute to the death of axotomized retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) following optic nerve crush (ONC) injury (Fernandes et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2012.

claim: JNK2/JNK3 or c-Jun deficiency is neuroprotective over the first two weeks after ONC but does not enable the sustained RGC survival provided by DLK deficiency.
source: JNK2/JNK3 or c-Jun deficiency is neuroprotective over the first two weeks after ONC but does not enable the sustained RGC survival provided by DLK deficiency (Fernandes et al., 2012; Watkins et al., 2013; Welsbie et al., 2013), raising the possibility that DLK controls additional signaling pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2012; Watkins et al., 2013; Welsbie et al., 2013.

claim: Expression profiling of lumbar (L4) DRG 24 hr after sciatic nerve transection revealed injury-regulated mRNAs resembling those observed in similar studies of both peripheral and CNS axonal damage.
source: Expression profiling of lumbar (L4) DRG 24 hr after sciatic nerve transection revealed a number of injury-regulated mRNAs resembling those observed in similar studies of both peripheral and CNS axonal damage (Hu et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Stam et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2007; Yasuda et al., 2014), including our previous study of ONC (Watkins et al., 2013) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Stam et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2007; Yasuda et al., 2014; Watkins et al., 2013, and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: ISR-associated mRNAs, including Atf4, Chac1, and Eif4ebp1, are present in both SNC and ONC models.
source: In addition to known c-Jun-dependent expression changes (Fernandes et al., 2013), in both models we noted the presence of ISR-associated mRNAs, including Atf4 and its target genes Chac1 and Eif4ebp1 (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Mungrue et al., 2009; Yamaguchi et al., 2008), as well as Eif2ak3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), but not other eIF2α kinases (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2013; Mungrue et al., 2009; Yamaguchi et al., 2008, and shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression changes observed in an ISR-related gene set is greater than would be expected by chance in both SNC and ONC axonal injury models.
source: Further analysis comparing nerve injury-induced mRNAs to genes known to be upregulated in an ATF4-dependent manner after neuronal oxidative stress (Lange et al., 2008) revealed that the expression changes observed in this ISR-related gene set is greater than would be expected by chance in both axonal injury models (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lange et al., 2008, and shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: Immunoblot analysis revealed a robust elevation of ATF4 after sciatic nerve crush injury.
source: In addition to the expected phosphorylation of c-Jun indicative of stress-responsive JNK signaling, immunoblot analysis revealed a robust elevation of the transcription factor ATF4 after injury (Figure 1e), consistent with activation of the ISR.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Potential increases in the levels of PERK, p-PERK, and p-eIF2α were noted over multiple experiments and time points after sciatic nerve crush.
source: We also noted potential increases in the levels of PERK, the phosphorylated form of PERK (p-PERK) and its target eIF2α (p-eIF2α) over multiple experiments and time points, although as noted previously in assessments of PERK signaling (Qi et al., 2011), the changes in these markers were less definitive than those observed with ATF4.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to Qi et al., 2011.

claim: A significant upregulation of ATF4 was found in retina following ONC, along with more modest and variable elevation of p-PERK and p-eIF2α.
source: We found a similarly significant upregulation of ATF4 in retina following ONC, along with more modest and variable elevation of p-PERK and p-eIF2α (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Withdrawal of NGF from cultured embryonic DRG neurons results in induction of JNK signaling and the ISR, as shown by activation of PERK and ATF4.
source: We observed that NGF withdrawal results in induction of not only JNK signaling, as previously described (Sengupta Ghosh et al., 2011), but also the ISR, as shown by activation of PERK and ATF4 (Figure 1g), and an elevation in the phosphorylated form of eIF2α.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sengupta Ghosh et al., 2011, and shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Knockdown of Eif2ak3 consistently abrogated the upregulation of ATF4 following NGF deprivation in embryonic DRG cultures.
source: Whereas targeting Eif2ak1, Eif2ak2, or Eif2ak4 resulted in modest, variable effects on ATF4 protein levels, knockdown of Eif2ak3 consistently abrogated the upregulation of ATF4, suggesting that PERK is largely responsible for this effect (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Knockdown of ATF4 enhances axon regeneration in adult sensory neurons in vitro.
source: By quantifying neurite growth of these adult sensory neurons on a growth-restrictive substrate over two days in culture, we found that knockdown of ATF4 enhances axon regeneration (Figure 1i and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1i and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Eif4ebp1 and Chac1 mRNA are persistently upregulated over the first three days after sciatic nerve crush.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of L4 DRG showed the persistent upregulation of eIF4E binding protein-1 (Eif4ebp1) and Chac1 mRNA over the first three days, whereas Ddit3 and Ppp1r15a mRNA, initially elevated, returned to near baseline levels by the second day (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Ddit3 and Ppp1r15a mRNA, initially elevated after sciatic nerve crush, returned to near baseline levels by the second day.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of L4 DRG showed the persistent upregulation of eIF4E binding protein-1 (Eif4ebp1) and Chac1 mRNA over the first three days, whereas Ddit3 and Ppp1r15a mRNA, initially elevated, returned to near baseline levels by the second day (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Eif4ebp1 and Chac1 exhibit at least partial ATF4-dependence after sciatic nerve crush.
source: Evaluation of L4 DRGs from ATF4-deficient (Yoshizawa et al., 2009) and wildtype control mice (see Supplemental Methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2) revealed at least partial ATF4-dependence of Eif4ebp1 and Chac1 but not Ddit3 and Ppp1r15a (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yoshizawa et al., 2009, and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Ddit3 and Ppp1r15a do not exhibit ATF4-dependence after sciatic nerve crush.
source: Evaluation of L4 DRGs from ATF4-deficient (Yoshizawa et al., 2009) and wildtype control mice (see Supplemental Methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2) revealed at least partial ATF4-dependence of Eif4ebp1 and Chac1 but not Ddit3 and Ppp1r15a (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yoshizawa et al., 2009, and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: ISRIB administration prevented the upregulation of ATF4 protein in L3/L4 DRG after sciatic nerve crush but did not alter p-c-Jun induction.
source: ISRIB administration prevented the upregulation of ATF4 protein in L3/L4 DRG after SNC but did not alter p-c-Jun induction (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: ISRIB treatment significantly reduced Chac1 and Eif4ebp1 mRNA, but not Ppp1r15a and Ddit3 mRNA in L4 DRG following sciatic nerve crush.
source: Consistent with this observation and our data in ATF4-deficient mice, ISRIB treatment significantly reduced Chac1 and Eif4ebp1 mRNA, but not Ppp1r15a and Ddit3 mRNA in L4 DRG following SNC (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d.

claim: All four mRNAs (Chac1, Eif4ebp1, Ppp1r15a, and Ddit3) are induced by NGF withdrawal in embryonic DRG cultures.
source: As was observed following SNC, all four mRNAs are induced by NGF withdrawal, yet the regulation of these targets in this model exhibits distinct ISR-dependence.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Chac1, Eif4ebp1, Ppp1r15a, and Ddit3 mRNA exhibit ISRIB sensitivity following NGF withdrawal in embryonic DRG cultures.
source: In this instance, not only Chac1 and Eif4ebp1 mRNA, but also Ppp1r15a and Ddit3 mRNA, exhibit ISRIB sensitivity (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2e.

claim: ISRIB treatment did not impact the levels of phospho-c-Jun following sciatic nerve crush.
source: In considering whether PERK may mediate neurodegeneration through stimulation of DLK/JNK signaling, we noted that ISRIB treatment did not impact the levels of phospho-c-Jun following SNC, suggesting that DLK/JNK signaling is not downstream of PERK (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The induction of p-c-Jun is unaltered in ATF4-deficient mice after sciatic nerve crush.
source: Accordingly, the induction of p-c-Jun is unaltered in ATF4-deficient mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The absence of DLK prevents c-Jun phosphorylation and upregulation of ATF4 after sciatic nerve crush.
source: Immunoblots of L3/L4 DRG demonstrated that the absence of DLK prevents not only c-Jun phosphorylation but also upregulation of ATF4 after SNC (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Not only ATF4-independent (Ppp1r15a and Ddit3) but also ATF4-mediated expression changes (Eif4ebp1 and Chac1) exhibited DLK-dependence after sciatic nerve crush.
source: Consistent with this, qRT-PCR analysis revealed that not only ATF4-independent (Ppp1r15a and Ddit3) but also ATF4-mediated expression changes (Eif4ebp1 and Chac1) exhibited DLK-dependence (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3b.

claim: DLK is necessary for ISR-mediated effects following adult nerve injury in vivo.
source: These results indicate that DLK is necessary for ISR-mediated effects following adult nerve injury in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data.

claim: Inhibition of DLK reduced p-PERK and ATF4 induction, in addition to p-c-Jun, following NGF-withdrawal in primary DRG cultures.
source: Immunoblots of embryonic DRG neuron lysates revealed that DLK kinase inhibition using the selective inhibitor GNE-3511 (Patel et al., 2015) resulted in not only reduced p-c-Jun but also suppressed PERK phosphorylation and ATF4 upregulation (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Patel et al., 2015, and shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: NGF-deprived cultures treated with ISRIB specifically displayed reduced ATF4, but not p-PERK and p-c-Jun.
source: In contrast, NGF-deprived cultures treated with ISRIB specifically displayed reduced ATF4, but not p-PERK and p-c-Jun, as would be predicted for inhibition of the ISR downstream of both DLK and PERK (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: DLK-deficient embryonic DRG neurons displayed no induction of p-PERK or ATF4 following NGF withdrawal.
source: DLK-deficient embryonic DRG neurons (Sengupta Ghosh et al., 2011) confirmed the results observed with DLK inhibitor and displayed no induction of p-PERK or ATF4 following NGF withdrawal (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sengupta Ghosh et al., 2011, and shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: DLK overexpression in a doxycycline-inducible stable 293T cell line results in elevated ATF4 protein and a molecular weight shift in human PERK indicative of phosphorylation.
source: We found that DLK overexpression in a doxycycline-inducible stable 293T cell line (Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013) results in both elevated ATF4 protein and a molecular weight shift in human PERK indicative of phosphorylation (Axten et al., 2012) (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013 and Axten et al., 2012, and shown in Figure 3e.

claim: DLK activity is required for DLK-mediated activation of PERK, c-Jun, and ATF4 in HEK293 cells.
source: DLK activity is required for this effect, as increasing concentrations of DLK inhibitor reduced DLK-mediated activation of PERK, c-Jun, and ATF4, whereas ISRIB selectively blocked ATF4 induction (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3e.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing wildtype DLK, but not a kinase-dead mutant (S302A) of DLK, resulted in upregulation of ATF4 protein levels.
source: Furthermore, HEK293T cells expressing wildtype DLK, but not a kinase-dead mutant (S302A) of DLK, resulted in upregulation of ATF4 protein levels (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3f.

claim: DLK activity is both necessary and sufficient for initiating both the ISR and JNK signaling.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that DLK activity is both necessary and sufficient for initiating both the ISR and JNK signaling, with both contributing to neurodegeneration following acute insults.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data.

claim: Activation of the ISR is a novel component of the broad DLK-mediated stress response.
source: Activation of the ISR is therefore a novel component of the broad DLK-mediated stress response.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data.

claim: Suppression of ATF4 protein upregulation was found in JNK2/3-deficient DRGs after sciatic nerve crush.
source: As observed for DLK-deficiency, we found suppression of ATF4 protein upregulation in JNK2/3-deficient DRGs after SNC (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both DLK and JNK are necessary for ISR activation after injury.
source: These results demonstrate that both DLK and JNK are necessary for ISR activation after injury.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data.

claim: Associated sciatic nerve segments did not exhibit clear evidence of ATF4 and p-PERK after sciatic nerve crush.
source: In contrast to the elevated p-PERK and ATF4 levels observed in L3/L4 DRGs, associated sciatic nerve segments did not exhibit clear evidence of ATF4 and p-PERK, and the marginal signal sometimes detected in nerve could potentially represent induction of the ISR in neighboring cells rather than axons (Mantuano et al., 2011) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mantuano et al., 2011, and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: p-PERK and ATF4 increase over the first six hours following NGF withdrawal in the chamber containing cell bodies and proximal axons, but the corresponding distal axons did not exhibit detectable levels of either.
source: Although p-PERK and ATF4 increase over the first six hours following NGF withdrawal in the chamber containing cell bodies and proximal axons, the corresponding distal axons did not exhibit detectable levels of either (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Distal axonal NGF deprivation is sufficient to result in elevated ATF4 protein in the central compartment containing NGF-treated DRG cell bodies and proximal axons.
source: Consistent with our observations following nerve crush in vivo, we observed that distal axonal NGF deprivation is sufficient to result in elevated ATF4 protein in the central compartment containing NGF-treated DRG cell bodies and proximal axons (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Inhibition of JNK signaling in either the central or distal chambers prevented the induction of ATF4 following distal axonal NGF deprivation.
source: Inhibition of JNK signaling in either the central or distal chambers prevented the induction of ATF4.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: ISRIB only prevented ATF4 induction when applied to the central compartment following distal axonal NGF deprivation.
source: In contrast, ISRIB only had this effect when applied centrally (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d.

claim: ISR activation occurs after JNK-mediated retrograde signaling.
source: Together, these data do not preclude a role for low levels of axonally translated ATF4 in regulating acute injury responses (Baleriola et al., 2014) but suggest a prominent contribution of PERK activity that occurs after JNK-mediated retrograde signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data and supported by a citation to Baleriola et al., 2014.

claim: Reducing c-Jun expression by siRNA in DRG neurons does not reduce induction of ATF4 upon NGF deprivation.
source: We therefore asked if upregulation of ATF4 protein is influenced by the levels of c-Jun, finding that reducing c-Jun expression by siRNA in DRG neurons does not reduce induction of ATF4 upon NGF deprivation (Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: DLK does not control activation of the ISR primarily through c-Jun-mediated transcriptional changes.
source: Although a small increase in ATF4 transcription can be observed following nerve crush (Figure 1b), these results are consistent with the central role for translational control of ATF4 implied by ISRIB sensitivity and suggest that DLK does not control activation of the ISR primarily through c-Jun-mediated transcriptional changes.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: An ISR-related gene set representing putative ATF4-dependent transcripts is enriched in the NGF deprivation neuronal stress model.
source: Nevertheless, we found that, as in the ONC and SNC models, an ISR-related gene set representing putative ATF4-dependent transcripts (Lange et al., 2008) is enriched in this neuronal stress model (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lange et al., 2008, and shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Chac1, Eif4ebp1, Ppp1r15a, Ddit3 were among a group of 1130 mRNAs that reached a strict criterion for expression change following NGF deprivation.
source: We further examined the ISR genes that we had previously evaluated by qPCR, confirming that Chac1, Eif4ebp1, Ppp1r15a, Ddit3 were, along with Jun, among a group of 1130 mRNAs that reached a strict criterion (>1.5 fold, adjusted p<0.001) for expression change following NGF deprivation (Figure 5b and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: About two-thirds of expression changes following NGF deprivation were significantly reduced in the presence of DLKi.
source: We next examined this group of expression changes for DLK-dependence, finding that about two-thirds were significantly reduced in the presence of DLKi (Figure 5c and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: Over 80% of the 581 upregulated RNAs following NGF deprivation exhibited DLKi sensitivity that reached statistical significance.
source: Further analysis revealed that the DLK-dependence is particularly enriched among upregulated RNAs, with over 80% of the 581 upregulated RNAs exhibiting DLKi sensitivity that reached statistical significance (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c.

claim: DLK-mediated stress signaling following NGF deprivation contributes more prominently to induction of stress responsive genes than to downregulation of neuronal gene expression.
source: Together these findings argue that DLK-mediated stress signaling following NGF deprivation contributes more prominently to induction of stress responsive genes than to downregulation of neuronal gene expression (e.g., the transcription factor Pou4f2), distinct from the influential role of DLK in both up- and down-regulated mRNAs previously observed in ONC (Watkins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data and supported by a citation to Watkins et al., 2013.

claim: Approximately half of the DLKi-sensitive expression changes exhibit ISRIB sensitivity.
source: Approximately half of the DLKi-sensitive expression changes exhibit ISRIB sensitivity (Figure 5c), indicating the ISR is a major component of the DLK-mediated stress response, including pro-apoptotic genes (e.g., Bbc3, which encodes the protein PUMA) (Simon et al., 2016) (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5d, and supported by a citation to Simon et al., 2016.

claim: The ISR is a major component of the DLK-mediated stress response.
source: Approximately half of the DLKi-sensitive expression changes exhibit ISRIB sensitivity (Figure 5c), indicating the ISR is a major component of the DLK-mediated stress response, including pro-apoptotic genes (e.g., Bbc3, which encodes the protein PUMA) (Simon et al., 2016) (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data and supported by a citation to Simon et al., 2016.

claim: A substantial number of DLK-mediated expression changes exhibit little to no ISR-dependence, including apoptotic regulators such as Bcl2l11 and Dusp16.
source: Importantly, however, a substantial number of DLK-mediated expression changes exhibit little to no ISR-dependence, including additional apoptotic regulators, such as Bcl2l11, which encodes the protein Bim, (Biswas et al., 2007) and Dusp16 (Maor-Nof et al., 2016) (Figure 5d and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5d and Figure 5—source data 1, and supported by citations to Biswas et al., 2007 and Maor-Nof et al., 2016.

claim: Of the approximately 50% of upregulated mRNAs suppressed by ISRIB, 85% also exhibit statistically significant DLKi sensitivity.
source: Of the approximately 50% of upregulated mRNAs suppressed by ISRIB, 85% also exhibit statistically significant DLKi sensitivity (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c.

claim: ISRIB treatment is sufficient to reduce degeneration at 16 h following NGF deprivation in DRG explants.
source: We observed that, similar to inhibition of DLK (GNE-3511, 100 nM) (Patel et al., 2015) and JNK (JNKi, AS601245, 1 µM) (Carboni et al., 2004), ISRIB treatment is sufficient to reduce degeneration at 16 h (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a,b and supported by citations to Patel et al., 2015 and Carboni et al., 2004.

claim: In contrast to DLK/JNK inhibition, protection by ISRIB is not sustained at 20 h following NGF deprivation in DRG explants.
source: However, in contrast to DLK/JNK inhibition, this protection is not sustained at 20 h (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6c,d.

claim: Axonal protection by ISRIB is mirrored by a delay in the apoptosis marker activated Caspase-3 in NGF-deprived dissociated DRG cultures, with a reduction that is similar to DLKi at 7 h but is less pronounced after 8 h.
source: We further found that axonal protection by ISRIB is mirrored by a delay in the apoptosis marker activated Caspase-3 in NGF-deprived dissociated DRG cultures, with a reduction that is similar to DLKi at 7 h but is less pronounced after 8 h (Figure 6e,f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6e,f.

claim: ISR activity contributes to neurodegeneration following NGF deprivation.
source: These data provide evidence that ISR activity contributes to neurodegeneration, though, consistent with the ISR controlling only a subset of expression changes downstream of retrograde DLK/JNK signaling, its disruption is less protective than inhibiting DLK/JNK in this rapidly degenerating in vitro model.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data.

claim: Genetic disruption of DLK resulted in attenuation of ATF4 protein induction following optic nerve crush.
source: Consistent with our data in other models, genetic disruption DLK resulted in attenuation of both ATF4 protein induction (Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and Chac1, Eif4ebp1, Ddit3, and Ppp1r15a mRNA upregulation (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genetic disruption of DLK resulted in attenuation of Chac1, Eif4ebp1, Ddit3, and Ppp1r15a mRNA upregulation following optic nerve crush.
source: Consistent with our data in other models, genetic disruption DLK resulted in attenuation of both ATF4 protein induction (Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and Chac1, Eif4ebp1, Ddit3, and Ppp1r15a mRNA upregulation (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Mice lacking JNK2 and JNK3 lack induction of Chac1, Eif4ebp1, Ddit3, and Ppp1r15a mRNAs following optic nerve crush.
source: Mice lacking JNK2 and JNK3 also lack induction of these mRNAs (Figure 7c), further supporting the notion that DLK/JNK signaling is necessary for ISR activation following ONC, as it is following SNC or NGF deprivation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Examination of Syn1-Cre/Eif2ak3lx/lx retinas three days after nerve crush injury revealed a clear suppression of Chac1 mRNA induction.
source: Examination of Syn1-Cre/Eif2ak3lx/lx retinas three days after nerve crush injury revealed a clear suppression of Chac1 mRNA induction (Figure 7d), arguing that neuronal PERK mediates the DLK-dependent ISR.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Neuronal PERK mediates the DLK-dependent ISR following optic nerve crush.
source: Examination of Syn1-Cre/Eif2ak3lx/lx retinas three days after nerve crush injury revealed a clear suppression of Chac1 mRNA induction (Figure 7d), arguing that neuronal PERK mediates the DLK-dependent ISR.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data and shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Systemic ISRIB dosing resulted in a significant reduction in ATF4 protein induction in retina following optic nerve crush.
source: We found that, as in SNC, systemic ISRIB dosing resulted in a significant reduction in ATF4 protein induction in retina following ONC (Figure 7e and Figure 7—figure supplement 3), as well as reduced Chac1 mRNA upregulation (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7e and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Systemic ISRIB dosing resulted in reduced Chac1 mRNA upregulation in retina following optic nerve crush.
source: We found that, as in SNC, systemic ISRIB dosing resulted in a significant reduction in ATF4 protein induction in retina following ONC (Figure 7e and Figure 7—figure supplement 3), as well as reduced Chac1 mRNA upregulation (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7f.

claim: Intravitreal injection of an AAV2 vector driving expression of an shRNA targeting Atf4 partially suppressed Chac1 mRNA induction following optic nerve crush.
source: Similarly, intravitreal injection of an AAV2 vector driving expression of both GFP and an shRNA targeting Atf4 partially suppressed Chac1 mRNA induction (Figure 7g and Figure 7—figure supplement 4) but not Jun mRNA upregulation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7g and Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Intravitreal injection of an AAV2 vector driving expression of an shRNA targeting Atf4 did not suppress Jun mRNA upregulation following optic nerve crush.
source: Similarly, intravitreal injection of an AAV2 vector driving expression of both GFP and an shRNA targeting Atf4 partially suppressed Chac1 mRNA induction (Figure 7g and Figure 7—figure supplement 4) but not Jun mRNA upregulation.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Neuronal PERK deficiency provides partial but significant neuroprotection two weeks after optic nerve crush.
source: Assessment RGC survival two weeks after ONC in Syn1-Cre/Eif2ak3lx/lx mice (Figure 8a) revealed that neuronal PERK deficiency provides partial but significant neuroprotection, when assessed either by blind scoring of axonal density within the retina (Figure 8b) or by automated quantitative assessment of RGC survival, with the proportion of remaining γ-synuclein+, βIII-tubulin (TuJ1)+ RGCs increasing from 42% to 72% (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8a,b.

claim: Daily dosing with ISRIB (10 mg/kg) for ten days can provide partial neuroprotection in the optic nerve crush model.
source: Additionally, although microphthalmia in ATF4-deficient mice precluded ONC in that genetic model (Masuoka and Townes, 2002), we found that daily dosing with ISRIB (10 mg/kg) for ten days (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) can also provide partial neuroprotection in this model (Figure 8c,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8c,d and Figure 8—figure supplement 1, and supported by a citation to Masuoka and Townes, 2002.

claim: The PERK-mediated ISR cell-autonomously contributes to DLK-mediated neurodegenerative stress responses following acute neuronal insults.
source: Taken together, our current findings argue that the PERK-mediated ISR cell-autonomously contributes to DLK-mediated neurodegenerative stress responses following acute neuronal insults.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the preceding data.

claim: Following acute neuronal injury, JNK signaling and the ISR are tightly linked via the neuronal MAP kinase kinase kinase DLK.
source: The observations reported here reveal that following acute neuronal injury, these seemingly distinct cellular stress response pathways are tightly linked via the neuronal MAP kinase kinase kinase DLK.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the data presented in the study.

claim: The ISR-activating kinase PERK contributes to DLK-mediated gene expression changes and neurodegeneration.
source: We found that the ISR-activating kinase PERK contributes to DLK-mediated gene expression changes and neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the data presented in the study.

claim: Activation of PERK represents a second functional component, along with JNK signaling, of the DLK-driven stress response that regulates the fates of distressed neurons.
source: Thus, activation of PERK represents a second functional component, along with JNK signaling, of the DLK-driven stress response that regulates the fates of distressed neurons (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the data presented in the study and shown in Figure 9.

claim: Greater than 80% of ISRIB-sensitive expression changes are also DLKi-sensitive following NGF deprivation.
source: Furthermore, our RNA-seq data suggest that greater than 80% of ISRIB-sensitive expression changes are also DLKi-sensitive.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: c-Jun deficiency and PERK deficiency are each partially neuroprotective after optic nerve crush.
source: c-Jun deficiency (Fernandes et al., 2012) and PERK deficiency are each partially neuroprotective after ONC, and the control of both of these pro-apoptotic signaling pathways by DLK is consistent with the potent neuroprotection provided by DLK disruption (Watkins et al., 2013; Welsbie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2012; Watkins et al., 2013; Welsbie et al., 2013.

claim: The control of both c-Jun and PERK pro-apoptotic signaling pathways by DLK is consistent with the potent neuroprotection provided by DLK disruption.
source: c-Jun deficiency (Fernandes et al., 2012) and PERK deficiency are each partially neuroprotective after ONC, and the control of both of these pro-apoptotic signaling pathways by DLK is consistent with the potent neuroprotection provided by DLK disruption (Watkins et al., 2013; Welsbie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Watkins et al., 2013; Welsbie et al., 2013.

claim: A distinct PERK-independent branch of the UPR is only transiently activated after optic nerve crush.
source: However, a distinct PERK-independent branch of the UPR is only transiently activated after ONC (Hu et al., 2012), and protein synthesis inhibitors fail to prevent PERK activation during neuronal ischemia (Sanderson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2012 and Sanderson et al., 2010.

claim: Protein synthesis inhibitors fail to prevent PERK activation during neuronal ischemia.
source: However, a distinct PERK-independent branch of the UPR is only transiently activated after ONC (Hu et al., 2012), and protein synthesis inhibitors fail to prevent PERK activation during neuronal ischemia (Sanderson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sanderson et al., 2010.

claim: PERK activation occurs downstream of DLK/JNK-mediated retrograde injury signaling.
source: Our findings from Campenot chamber experiments suggests that PERK activation occurs downstream of DLK/JNK-mediated retrograde injury signaling, though additional experiments suggest that it is not dependent on c-Jun.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the Campenot chamber experiments.

claim: PERK activation is not dependent on c-Jun.
source: Our findings from Campenot chamber experiments suggests that PERK activation occurs downstream of DLK/JNK-mediated retrograde injury signaling, though additional experiments suggest that it is not dependent on c-Jun.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on additional experiments.

claim: PERK signaling can be triggered by the MAP kinase DLK following acute neuronal insults.
source: Our findings reveal that PERK signaling, which is initiated by ER stress as one branch of the UPR, can also be triggered by the MAP kinase DLK following acute neuronal insults.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the data presented in the study.

claim: DLK activation is sufficient to activate PERK.
source: Our observation that DLK activation is sufficient to activate PERK suggests the possibility that activation of the ISR may be a common consequence of MAP kinase stress signaling in DLK-expressing cells, such as neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the data presented in the study.

claim: Activation of the ISR may be a common consequence of MAP kinase stress signaling in DLK-expressing cells.
source: Our observation that DLK activation is sufficient to activate PERK suggests the possibility that activation of the ISR may be a common consequence of MAP kinase stress signaling in DLK-expressing cells, such as neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DLK activation is sufficient to activate PERK.

claim: JNK activation has been noted in many models of progressive neurodegeneration.
source: Although the precise role(s) of DLK in neurodegenerative diseases requires further investigation, JNK activation has been noted in many models of progressive neurodegeneration (Coffey, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coffey, 2014.

claim: DLK activity may influence or mediate PERK signaling in models of progressive neurodegeneration.
source: It is therefore possible that DLK activity influences or mediates PERK signaling in these settings.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that JNK activation has been noted in many models of progressive neurodegeneration.

claim: Blocking DLK activity may provide an appealing therapeutic strategy for simultaneously targeting pro-degenerative PERK and JNK signaling in neurons.
source: Given the neuronally restricted expression of DLK (Hirai et al., 2006) and the viability of adult DLK-deficient mice (Watkins et al., 2013), blocking DLK activity may provide an appealing therapeutic strategy for simultaneously targeting pro-degenerative PERK and JNK signaling in neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Hirai et al., 2006 and Watkins et al., 2013.
